title: The Greatest Enemy
author: Michael Perrone
summary: Perrone argues that the widely-assumed sequence—reform institutions first, and personal/relational formation will follow—has the causality backwards. Drawing on his ongoing Build the Village project, he contends that all historically formative institutions were themselves born out of high-trust, high-demand relationships, so relational renewal must precede institutional renewal, not the other way around. He identifies radical individualism as the primary internal saboteur of this project: a cultural script, embraced across the political spectrum, that treats every relationship as revocable the moment it conflicts with personal authenticity or convenience. Perrone traces two versions of this individualism—the therapeutic snowflake identity and the more masculine-coded rugged individual archetype—and argues both make demanding, formative relationships nearly impossible to sustain. He closes by rejecting nostalgia or anti-technology retreat, instead proposing that modern comforts and thick relational/communal life are compatible if people are willing to accept the burden of compromise, inconvenience, and deference that close relationships require.
points: Perrone's central claim inverts the conventional wisdom: he argues formative institutions are downstream of high-trust relationships, not the reverse, so relational work has to come first.

He identifies radical individualism—including a masculine-coded self-sufficient man archetype—as the deepest obstacle to rebuilding thick community, because it treats every relational obligation as optional.
The essay reframes the enemy of renewal as internal rather than external: not political rivals or institutions, but each person's own habitual avoidance of demanding relationships.
Perrone explicitly rejects both nostalgia for a simpler past and anti-modern retreat, arguing instead that modern comfort and demanding communal life can coexist.
quotes: It turns out that demanding relationships are demanding and we are out of practice. So when offered the choice between it and a substitution, some cheap plastic, Chinese brand knock off, it's quite tempting to go with the knock off.

Consider, the archetypes of the rugged individual, the resourceful guy who doesn't need anyone, the man who just wants to be left alone, the parents dedicated to their own set of rules and pursuits, or the online mutuals who have a deep connection to their esoteric knowledge.
Culturally, we hold this idea of radical individualism so sacred that there's essentially no relationship which can't be justly severed if it's not in service to being authentically ourselves.

When the world is full of radical individuals, as it is now, institutions themselves lose the relational context to form anyone. All that's left to do is for mass institutions to herd us about, like the powerless cattle we are.
I believe I can have my cake and eat it too. That I can retain almost all of the amazing benefits of modern life while also enjoying the fruits of demanding family and communal relationships.
As good as formative relationships sound to the ear, it comes with the burden of compromise, inconvenience, and deference.
